To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ability to remember information in the past can be predicted by the engagement of the same brain regions during the initial presentation of information (encoding) and when the information is retrieved (retrieval).

neural patterns of activity that predict memory function during one phase of memory can be used to predict memory function during other phases of memory, and that combining neural patterns of activity from different phases of memory can improve the prediction of memory function.
the same neural patterns that predict successful encoding and retrieval of episodic memories can be identified in the same brain regions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the neural mechanisms that support human memory.
how the brain supports the ability to remember past experiences.
how the brain encodes and stores memories.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the engagement of the core MTL network, which is common to encoding, consolidation and retrieval, shapes the ability to form new episodic memories.
the engagement of common neural structures across the brain during encoding and retrieval are necessary for successful memory function.
the brain is an organ of the nervous system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
successful memory is predicted by a combination of common and distinct neural processes during encoding and retrieval.
the neural activity that predicts episodic memory function is similar across encoding and retrieval, despite differences in the neural dynamics that facilitate encoding and recall.
the engagement of the core memory network during encoding or retrieval is necessary for successful memory function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the engagement of common neural networks during encoding and retrieval can predict memory performance.
the brain’s ability to engage a common network of structures during encoding and retrieval is a critical component to the formation and retrieval of memories.
memory function is supported by common patterns of neural processing during encoding and retrieval that can be identified across the brain.
